## Biodiversity in figures: birds, flora and threatened species

Numbers, when looked at closely, tell a story of resilience. La Charca de Suárez is home to more than two hundred species of birds throughout the year, a figure that places this coastal wetland among the hotspots of Andalusian ornithology. Of that total, fifty nest regularly in its waters and reed beds, making the site a first-rate natural breeding ground for the avifauna of the Mediterranean coast. This is not simply a place of passage: it is a stable home where entire generations of birds complete their reproductive cycle.

Among the species that find refuge in the Charca, three names concentrate the attention of conservationists. The marbled teal (*Marmaronetta angustirostris*), a diving duck with mottled plumage that ranks among the most threatened Anatidae in Europe, uses the shallow water sheets to feed and reproduce. The white-headed duck (*Oxyura leucocephala*), with its characteristic sky-blue bill in males during the breeding season, has found in this corner of Granada one of its few remaining strongholds on the Iberian Peninsula. The aquatic warbler (*Acrocephalus paludicola*), a small passerine with elusive habits, completes the trio of emblematic species that alone justify the protection of the area.

The presence of these birds is no coincidence. It responds to a combination of ecological factors that the Charca has managed to preserve despite the urban pressure of its surroundings. The fresh waters from the Vega de Motril, mixed with the saline influence of the nearby Mediterranean, generate a salinity gradient that favours the proliferation of aquatic invertebrates. This trophic resource sustains waterbird populations throughout the year, but especially during the breeding season, when energy demands soar.

The annual censuses carried out by the Estación Ornitológica de la Charca add a further dimension to the wetland's value. During migratory passages, observers have recorded peaks of up to ten thousand birds concentrated in an area that barely exceeds fourteen hectares. The figure becomes even more impressive when one considers that we are talking about an urban wetland, surrounded by greenhouses and industrial estates. In spring and autumn, migratory waders, ducks and passerines find here an essential stopover point for rest and refuelling on their route between Europe and Africa.

The wetland's flora plays a structural role that often goes unnoticed by the occasional visitor. The reed beds of *Phragmites australis* form dense masses that act as a physical barrier against the wind and as support for the nesting of numerous species. The tamarisks (*Tamarix* spp.), with their flexible branches and tolerance to salinity, colonise the transition zones between water and dry land. The rushes complete a plant mosaic that provides shelter, food and breeding sites for a biological community much broader than the birds alone suggest.

That community includes a rich entomofauna that forms the base of the wetland's food chain. The aquatic and terrestrial insects associated with marsh vegetation feed insectivorous birds, but also the amphibians that inhabit the Charca. The Mediterranean tree frog (*Hyla meridionalis*), a small bright green arboreal frog, finds in the reed beds and tamarisks the ideal habitat to complete its life cycle. Its presence is a biological indicator of the environmental quality of the area, since amphibians are especially sensitive to pollution and alterations in the water regime.

The interaction between flora and fauna creates an ecological web that transcends mere coexistence. The reed beds filter nutrients from the water, preventing eutrophication processes that would degrade habitat quality. The roots of tamarisks and rushes stabilise sediments and prevent bank erosion. In return, birds disperse seeds and contribute organic matter that enriches the substrate. This dynamic balance is what allows the Charca to maintain its biological productivity year after year without large-scale artificial interventions.

The biodiversity data yielded by La Charca de Suárez takes on another dimension when contextualised within the Andalusian panorama. The Granada coast has lost most of its coastal wetlands over the last century, victims of agricultural and urban expansion. Every surviving hectare represents an irreplaceable ecological heritage, a link in the network of natural spaces connecting Doñana with the wetlands of the southeastern peninsula. The forthcoming designation as a Special Protection Area for Birds would officially recognise what the censuses have been demonstrating for years.

The continuous monitoring carried out by the Estación Ornitológica makes it possible to detect population trends and respond quickly to potential threats. Records from recent seasons show encouraging stability in the breeding populations of the most sensitive species, although technicians insist on maintaining vigilance. The marbled teal, for example, remains listed as an endangered species in Spain, and its presence in the Charca depends on factors beyond local control, such as weather conditions in its wintering areas.

The value of the Charca as a natural laboratory is not limited to ornithology. Studies on marsh vegetation, sampling of aquatic invertebrates and amphibian monitoring generate scientific information that feeds conservation strategies at regional scale. The combination of a protected area with a permanent monitoring station turns the Motril wetland into a model of integrated management, where applied research translates into concrete decisions on water and vegetation management.

The numbers support what the residents of Motril already take for granted. More than two hundred species of birds, fifty regular breeders, migratory peaks of ten thousand individuals and a plant and animal community that sustains the whole. La Charca de Suárez is neither a relic of the past nor an administrative whim: it is a living ecosystem that demonstrates, with data on the table, that ecological restoration works when given time and resources. Biodiversity here does not remain a statistical abstraction; it is heard at dawn and observed in every corner of the wetland, tangible and close.
